en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 2.
The Training Rule on the Udosita (the Second Kathina):
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, monks would leave their robes in the hands of other monks and depart on a journey through the countryside wearing only their inner and upper garments.
Those robes, having been left for a long time, became moth-eaten.
The monks had to dry them in the sun.
While wandering about the dwellings, the Venerable Ānanda saw those bhikkhus drying those robes.
Having seen them, he approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, whose robes are these that have become so stained?"
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda complained, grumbled, and expressed his dissatisfaction, saying:
“How can these bhikkhus, having placed their robes in the hands of other bhikkhus, set out on a journey through the countryside wearing only their inner and upper robes?”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rebuked those bhikkhus in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, bhikkhus, that bhikkhus, having placed their robes in the hands of other bhikkhus, set out on a journey through the country wearing only their inner and upper robes?’—
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish men, monks, having placed their robes in the hands of other monks, set out on a journey through the countryside wearing only their inner and upper garments?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without faith…” [and so forth].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:

“When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if a monk should be separated from his three robes even for a single night, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was ill in Kosambī.
His relatives sent a messenger to that bhikkhu, saying:
"May the venerable sir come; we shall attend to him."
The bhikkhus also said this: “Go, friend; your relatives will attend to you.
He replied:
“Friends, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One—”
"One must not be separated from one's three robes. Now, I am ill;
I am unable to depart taking my three robes with me.
“I will not go,” they said.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and in that connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, to grant a monk who is ill the authorization not to be separated from his three robes.
And this, monks, is how it should be granted:

That sick monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and raised his joined palms, should speak as follows:”
‘Venerable sir, I am ill.
I am unable to depart taking my three robes with me.
Therefore, venerable sir, I request from the Saṅgha permission not to be separated from my three robes.’
A second time she should be asked;
a third time she should be asked.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This monk named so-and-so is ill.
He is not able to depart taking his three robes with him.’
He thus requests from the Saṅgha the authorization not to be separated from his three robes.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant the authorization not to be separated from the three robes to the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sir, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhu named so-and-so is ill;
he is unable to depart taking his three robes with him."
He thus requests from the Saṅgha the authorization not to be separated from his three robes.
The Saṅgha grants the authorization not to be separated from the three robes to the monk named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of granting the authorization not to be separated from the three robes to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha has granted the permission for the monk named so-and-so not to be separated from his three robes.
It is approved by the Sangha; therefore, it is silent.
“I maintain this to be so.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina period has been suspended, if a monk should be separated from his three robes for even a single night, except by the consent of the monks, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.”
"His robe is finished" means that for the monk,
the robe has been made, or it has been lost, or destroyed, or burnt, or the expectation of obtaining a robe has ceased.
"The kaṭhina has been removed" means...
If it has been brought out according to one of the eight headings, or if it has been brought out by the Saṅgha in the interim—
should a bhikkhu be separated from his three robes, that is, from the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), or the inner robe (antaravāsaka), even for a single night.
"Except by the consent of the Saṅgha" means setting aside the consent of the Saṅgha.
"It becomes an offense entailing relinquishment" means:
At dawn, it becomes subject to forfeiture.
It must be forfeited to the Saṅgha, to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be forfeited:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which was spent overnight apart from me except by the monks’ authorization, is to be relinquished;
I relinquish it to the Sangha. …pe…
"She should give" ... [and so on] ... "they should give" ... [and so on] ... "I give to the Venerable One."
A village has a single precinct or multiple precincts.
A dwelling has a single precinct or multiple precincts.
A granary has a single precinct or multiple precincts.
A gabled house has a single precinct or multiple precincts.
A multi-storied building has a single precinct or multiple precincts.
A palace has a single precinct or multiple precincts.
A village may have a single common area or multiple common areas.
A boat may have a single common area or multiple common areas.
A caravan may have a single common area or multiple common areas.
A field may have a single common access or multiple common accesses.
A threshing floor may have a single common access or multiple common accesses.
A monastery may have a single common access or multiple common accesses.
A monastery has a single precinct and multiple precincts.
The foot of a tree has a single precinct and multiple precincts.
An open space has a single precinct and multiple precincts.
A village with a single precinct means a village belonging to a single family that is enclosed by a boundary. Having deposited one’s robe within the village, one must reside within the village.
If it is unenclosed, one must reside in whichever house the robe has been deposited, or one must not depart from the reach of one’s hand.

There is a village belonging to various families that is enclosed by a wall. One must stay in the house where the robe has been deposited, or in the assembly hall, or at the base of the gate; one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.
When going to the assembly hall, having placed the robe within arm’s reach, one must stay in the assembly hall or at the base of the gate;
one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it. Having deposited the robe in the assembly hall, one must stay in the assembly hall or at the base of the gate; one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.
If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the house where the robe has been deposited, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.
If there is the residence of a single family that is enclosed, consisting of various rooms and various apartments, having deposited the robe within the residence, one must stay within the residence.
If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe has been deposited, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.

There is a dwelling belonging to various families that is enclosed, with various rooms and various apartments. In whichever room the robe has been placed, one must stay in that room or at the door; one must not go beyond arm’s reach.
If it is unenclosed, one must stay in whichever room the robe has been placed, or within arm’s reach; one must not go beyond arm’s reach.

There is a storehouse belonging to a single family that is enclosed, with separate rooms and separate apartments. Having deposited the robe within the storehouse, one must dwell within the storehouse.
If it is unenclosed, one must dwell in whichever room the robe has been deposited, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.

There is a storeroom belonging to various families that is enclosed, with various rooms and various apartments. In whichever room the robe has been placed, one must reside in that room, or at the threshold of the door, or within arm’s reach; one must not go beyond that range.
If it is unenclosed, one must reside in whichever room the robe has been placed, or within arm’s reach; one must not go beyond that range. There is a watchtower belonging to a single family;
having deposited the robe inside the watchtower, one must reside inside the watchtower.
If there is a dwelling belonging to various families, with separate rooms and separate apartments, one must stay in the room where the robe has been placed, or at the door, or within arm’s reach;
one must not leave that vicinity. If there is a multi-storied building belonging to a single family, having placed the robe inside the building, one must stay inside the building.

If there is a multi-storied building belonging to various families, with separate rooms and separate apartments, one must stay in the room where the robe has been placed, or at the door, or within arm’s reach; one must not leave that vicinity.
If there is a mansion belonging to a single family, having deposited the robe inside the mansion, one must stay inside the mansion.

If there is a mansion belonging to various families, consisting of various rooms and various apartments, one must stay in whichever room the robe has been deposited, or at the door; one must not go beyond the reach of the hand.
If there is a watchtower belonging to a single family, having deposited the robe inside the watchtower, one must stay inside the watchtower.
There is a house belonging to various families, with separate rooms and separate apartments. One must stay in the room where the robe has been placed, or at the door;
one must not leave the reach of one's hand. There is a boat belonging to a single family. Having deposited the robe inside the boat, one must stay inside the boat.

There is a boat belonging to various families, with separate cabins and separate compartments. One must stay in the compartment where the robe has been placed, or one must not leave the reach of one's hand.

If it is a caravan belonging to a single family, having deposited the robe in the caravan, one must not go more than seven *abbhantara*s away from it, either in front or behind; one must not go beyond the range of sight.
If it is a caravan belonging to various families, having deposited the robe in the caravan, one must not go beyond arm’s reach.
If it is a field belonging to a single family and enclosed by a fence, having deposited the robe within the field, one must remain within the field.
It is unenclosed; one must not leave the reach of one’s hand.
It is the field of various families and it is enclosed. Having deposited the robe within the field, one must either stay at the door or not leave the reach of one’s hand.
It is unenclosed; one must not leave the reach of one’s hand.
If there is a granary belonging to a single family that is enclosed, having deposited the robe inside the granary, one must reside inside the granary.
If it is unenclosed, one must not go beyond arm’s reach.
If there is a granary belonging to various families that is enclosed, having deposited the robe inside the granary, one must reside at the entrance or not go beyond arm’s reach.
If it is unenclosed, one must not go beyond arm’s reach.
If there is a monastery belonging to a single family that is enclosed, having deposited one's robe within the monastery, one must reside within the monastery.
If it is unenclosed, one must not go beyond arm’s reach.

If there is a monastery belonging to various families that is enclosed by a wall, one may deposit one’s robe inside the monastery and stay either at the gate or without departing from hand’s reach of it.
If it is unenclosed, one must not depart from hand’s reach of it.
If there is a dwelling belonging to a single family that is enclosed by a wall, having deposited one’s robe inside the dwelling, one must stay inside the dwelling.
If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the very monastery where the robe has been deposited, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.

If it is a monastery belonging to various families and is enclosed, one must stay in the very monastery where the robe has been deposited, or at the base of the door, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.
If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the very monastery where the robe has been deposited, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of it.
If it is the foot of a tree belonging to a single family, one may deposit one’s robe within the shade and stay within the shade during the time when the shadow extends all around at midday.
If it is the foot of a tree belonging to various families, one must not depart from the reach of one’s hand.
An open space with a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*) means that in a forest where there is no village, an area extending seven *abbhantara*s all around constitutes a single precinct.
Beyond that, there is no exemption from the formal procedure.
If one has stayed apart and perceives that one has stayed apart, except by the consent of the monks, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If one has stayed apart but is unsure of it, except by the consent of the monks, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

If he is separated [from his robe] while perceiving himself as not separated, except by formal authorization of the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If it has not been formally relinquished, yet he perceives it as having been relinquished … [and so on] … if it has not been given away, yet he perceives it as having been given away … [and so on] …
Perceiving what has not been lost as lost;
perceiving what has not been destroyed as destroyed;
perceiving what has not been burnt as burnt.

If one perceives that something has not been stolen when it has been stolen, except by the consent of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one uses a robe that should be relinquished without having relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives that one is separated from [one's robes] when one is not separated from them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the robe] has not been separated [from him], but he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the robe] has not been separated and he perceives it as not having been separated, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If he renounces it before dawn; if he gives it away; if it is lost; if it is destroyed; if it is burnt; if they take it by force; if they take it on trust;
by the consent of the Saṅgha;
in the case of one who is insane.
"Of the first offender":
the second training rule on the *udositaka* (second *kaṭhina*) is finished.
